summary: Provides a set of guidelines to aid in the secure operation of the Internet. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a list of safety tips for people who run machines on the Internet.

subtitle: Foundational security responsibilities for everyone participating in the Internet.

tldr.problem: The Internet is a cooperative system without central authority, but security risks are growing as connectivity expands. Every participant—users, service providers, and vendors—needs to understand their role in keeping the system secure.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC establishes six key principles: users must follow security policies and protect their data; service providers must secure their systems and communicate policies; vendors must provide sound systems with security controls; and everyone must cooperate and seek technical improvements.
tldr.outcome: Clear guidance on security responsibilities creates a shared understanding that security is everyone's concern, from individuals using accounts to organizations running networks to companies building systems.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Users, service providers, vendors, the entire Internet

today: RFC 1281 remains the foundational security guideline for Internet operations. As an Informational RFC, it established the principle that security is a shared responsibility across the entire Internet ecosystem. Its six principles continue to shape how Internet service providers, system administrators, software vendors, and users approach security.

sections.title: Why Security Matters on the Internet
sections.content:
The Internet is built on voluntary cooperation—no single entity controls it, and every participating network is responsible for its own security. This is the Internet's strength, but it is also fragile. Security rules cannot be enforced from the top down; they must be voluntary and mutually agreed upon.

However, Internet participation is optional: joining the Internet is a choice, and that choice carries an expectation to follow the community's rules and guidelines. When security is compromised, it affects not just one organization but the entire interconnected network.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet works because everyone agrees to help keep it safe. No one has a boss who can make them secure it, so safety depends on everyone doing their part.

sections.title: What Security Includes
sections.content:
The RFC defines security broadly as four things: protection of privacy (keeping information confidential), protection against unauthorized modification (ensuring data is not altered), protection against denial of service (making sure services remain available), and protection against unauthorized access (ensuring only authorized people can use systems).

These protections apply at every level: to individual user accounts, to organizational networks, to the Internet backbone, and to every software component in between.
sections.plainLanguage: Security is about keeping secrets secret, making sure information does not get changed, keeping services running, and making sure only the right people can use things.

sections.title: Individual User Responsibilities
sections.content:
Users are individually responsible for understanding the security policies of systems they use and are accountable for their own behavior. This is not a license for weak system administrators—unauthorized access is a crime under laws like the U.S. Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, regardless of how weak a system's protection is.

Users should protect their own data and help protect shared systems. This means selecting strong passwords and changing them periodically, respecting file access controls, and handling privileges responsibly. Sharing accounts and passwords is strongly discouraged because it breaks accountability.
sections.plainLanguage: Users have to follow the rules even if the rules are not perfectly enforced. Pick good passwords, keep them secret, and do not mess with other people's files.

sections.title: Organizational and Vendor Responsibilities
sections.content:
Service providers (organizations running networks and systems) are responsible for maintaining security and clearly communicating their security policies to users. They must evaluate systems for security before deploying them, describe security features, and cooperate with the community in reporting and fixing security flaws promptly.

Vendors and system developers must provide systems that are sound and embody adequate security controls. They have an obligation to repair security flaws they discover, and to help the Internet community respond to vulnerabilities in a timely manner. Building security in from the start is an obligation, not an afterthought.
sections.plainLanguage: Organizations running networks must tell people what the rules are and enforce them. Software companies must build security in and fix problems quickly when they find them.

sections.title: Cooperation and Technical Advancement
sections.content:
The Internet works as a cooperative system where sites notify each other of security problems, assist in tracking violators, and help law enforcement. Sites should respond promptly to security incidents and to security fixes from vendors. When breaches occur, sites are encouraged to help identify the violator and pursue accountability through appropriate sanctions.

Technical improvements must continue on two fronts: better basic mechanisms (stronger password systems, better authentication), and new security protocols for critical services like mail, file transfer, and telnet. Operating systems must place greater emphasis on security in their design and implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: When someone finds a security problem, everyone warns each other. Everyone works together to improve the tools that keep things safe.
